title: Exception Handling
description: Checked vs. unchecked exceptions, try/catch/finally, throw/throws, multi-catch, and try-with-resources.
objectives: Distinguish checked exceptions, unchecked exceptions, and Errors
Use try/catch/finally, throw, and throws correctly

content.heading: The Exception Hierarchy
content.body:
Java's Throwable hierarchy splits into Error (serious problems like OutOfMemoryError, not meant to be caught/handled by normal application code) and Exception. Exception itself splits into checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception other than RuntimeException — the compiler forces you to either catch them or declare them with throws on the method signature, e.g., IOException) and unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses, like NullPointerException or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — the compiler does not require handling them, since they typically represent programming bugs rather than expected, recoverable conditions).

A method that might throw a checked exception without catching it must declare that in its signature: void readFile() throws IOException { ... } — this propagates the responsibility to handle it up to the caller.

content.heading: try/catch/finally, Custom Exceptions, and try-with-resources
content.body:
try { ... } catch (SpecificException e) { ... } finally { ... } works as in most languages: finally always runs, whether or not an exception occurred. Multi-catch, catch (IOException | SQLException e) { ... }, handles several unrelated exception types identically in one clause. throw new SomeException("message") explicitly raises an exception; a custom exception is defined by extending Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked).

try-with-resources, try (Resource r = new Resource()) { ... }, automatically closes any resource implementing AutoCloseable (like FileReader or a database connection) when the block exits, even on an exception — eliminating the need for manual close() calls in a finally block, and avoiding the classic bug of a resource leak from a forgotten or exception-skipped close().

content.explanation: InsufficientFundsException is a custom unchecked exception carrying a clear message. try-with-resources guarantees reader is closed automatically, without a separate finally block.

keyPoints: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked (RuntimeException) exceptions don't require this
finally runs whether or not an exception occurred, and even if a return happens inside try/catch
Multi-catch (catch (A | B e)) handles multiple exception types in one clause
try-with-resources automatically closes any AutoCloseable resource, avoiding manual close() bookkeeping
commonMistakes: Catching an overly broad Exception and silently hiding a real bug
Forgetting to declare throws for a checked exception a method doesn't catch itself
Manually closing resources in a finally block instead of using try-with-resources, and getting the cleanup logic wrong on an early exception
